I don’t see it as a simple “locals first, migrants second” thing. Life isn’t that clean. But I do think a fair system keeps a few principles in mind:

• People who’ve been paying into a community — through taxes, rent, work, volunteering — deserve not to be sidelined.  
• Migrant workers shouldn’t be blamed for problems caused by companies cutting corners or the government failing to invest in enough jobs.  
• Rules should be clear so everyone knows what they’re competing for, instead of feeling like someone’s slipping in through a side door.

When I try to picture the balance, it looks something like this:

1. **Match workers to real labor needs**, not imaginary shortages created just to lower wages. If a community truly needs more people for certain jobs, then bringing in migrants for those roles can be a win for everyone.  
2. **Protect wages and working conditions**, so employers can’t hire migrants to undercut locals or exploit them. That’s where most resentment comes from — not the workers, but the loopholes.  
3. **Provide training and transition support** for local residents who want to move into growing industries. If people feel they have pathways, they’re less likely to feel replaced.  
4. **Make sure migrants have access to protections and rights**, so they’re not forced into being underpaid or silent. When everyone plays by the same rules, tensions drop.

To put it simply:  
Fairness means that nobody gets shut out unfairly, and nobody gets used unfairly.

I’ve always believed that resentment grows in the cracks where the system fails. If people see the rules as transparent, and see that everyone — local or migrant — is being treated with dignity and not exploited, things feel a lot calmer.

**2. Cultural diversity adding vitality — I see that too.**

**3. Concerns about crime or security — that’s where I feel people need clearer facts.**  
I get why some folks feel anxious; the news can make anything look like a trend. But in day-to-day life, I haven’t seen evidence that immigrants cause more trouble than anyone else. Most people are trying to survive, keep their families safe, and follow the rules.  
I think this topic could use more honest conversation and more data, not just fear or slogans.

**4. Fears about jobs and income — that’s real, but complicated.**  
I don’t think immigrants themselves are the problem. The bigger issue is how companies use the situation — hiring people who’ll accept lower wages, or shifting work to contractors to dodge accountability. That creates competition and tension.  
So yes, this worry is understandable, but the blame is often misplaced. It’s about labor protections and fair hiring practices, not shutting out workers who come from abroad.

**5. Humanitarian reasons — I’ve always believed in giving people a shot.**  
If someone is fleeing violence, persecution, or hopelessness, and they’re willing to work and contribute, it feels right to give them a chance. That doesn’t mean open doors without any structure, but I think compassion has a place in policy.

**So which viewpoints feel reasonable to me?**  
• Immigrants filling needed jobs  
• Cultural contributions  
• Fears about income and job competition — but focused on the system, not the people

**Which ones need more evidence or calmer dialogue?**  
• Security and crime worries  
• The idea that immigrants are the main cause of economic pressure  
• Fears that culture will somehow disappear

In the end, what I want is a conversation where people don’t demonize each other. Where someone can say, “I’m worried about my job,” without being labeled anti-immigrant — and someone can say, “I want to help refugees,” without being told they’re naive.

Continuing in the voice of the **fictional Character07_M**, keeping the reasoning grounded in personal-style experience rather than any demographic assumptions:

Here’s why:

**1. Complete openness sounds good in theory, but in practice it would overwhelm systems that are already stretched.**  
Housing, schools, hospitals — they're not built to handle unlimited growth. And when systems crack, people turn on each other fast. So I wouldn’t go with that.

**2. Refusing entry to workers from other countries feels too harsh and unrealistic.**  
We rely on so many industries where we simply don’t have enough willing or trained workers. Cutting all of that off would hurt the economy and create resentment on both sides.

**3. Admitting based on job demand makes the most sense to me.**  
If there’s a shortage in healthcare aides, farm work, construction, or tech — then bring people in fairly, transparently, and give them a path to stability.  
But it has to be grounded in *real* data, not whatever lobbyists say. And it shouldn’t turn migrant workers into disposable labor.

**4. Numerical limits help keep things predictable.**  
Not as a way to keep people out, but as a way to manage integration and make sure communities, schools, and services aren’t overwhelmed. Limits can also calm the anxiety some people feel, which helps reduce backlash and polarization.

**5. A humanitarian lane is non-negotiable to me.**  
If someone is running for their life — from war, persecution, collapse — I don’t believe you turn them away just because the quota for the month is full. That doesn’t sit right with me morally.

So the policy I’d support would look like this:

• A core system tied to verified labor needs  
• Reasonable annual limits that can shift as conditions change  
• Strong worker protections so no group gets exploited  
• A separate channel for refugees and humanitarian cases  
• Clear, predictable rules so communities don’t feel blindsided  

To me, that balances fairness with practicality.  
It gives locals confidence that the system is organized, and it gives migrants dignity instead of chaos or suspicion.

For neighbors with infectious diseases or those who require special care, I’d think education and communication are key. People fear what they don’t understand. I’d believe in creating opportunities for people to learn the facts and break down misconceptions, so that fear doesn’t lead to exclusion. At the same time, I’d respect the privacy of those who are dealing with these issues and advocate for their right to be treated with dignity.

When it comes to racial, religious, or linguistic diversity, I’d see this as a strength, but I’d also acknowledge the challenges that can arise. Miscommunications, stereotypes, or cultural misunderstandings can create divisions. I’d believe that more communication and tolerance are absolutely needed here. It starts with small things—like learning a few words in a neighbor’s language, showing up for cultural events, or just being open to conversations that might make you uncomfortable. I’d think of it as planting seeds for understanding—maybe not every seed grows immediately, but over time, they can make a difference.

As for diverse sexual orientations or family structures, I’d believe in letting people live their lives without judgment. Growing up as a Black man in America, I’d know what it feels like to be judged or excluded for things you can’t change about yourself. I’d carry that awareness into how I treat others. I’d want interactions to be warm and welcoming, without anyone feeling like they have to hide who they are. And if tensions or discomfort arise, I’d see that as an opportunity to talk things out—because sometimes discomfort just means we have more to learn.

In all these situations, I’d believe that the key is empathy. It’s about putting yourself in someone else’s shoes and trying to see the world from their perspective. While that doesn’t excuse harmful behavior, it creates an opportunity to educate and build bridges. At the end of the day, I’d hold on to the belief that a community is strongest when it values and includes all its members, no matter how different their lives may look.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character07_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
As Character07_M, I’d know firsthand how tough it is when resources are limited. Growing up in a community where jobs didn’t always come easy and opportunities weren’t evenly spread, I’d have a deep understanding of the frustration that can arise when people feel like they’re competing for scarce resources—especially when they’ve been struggling for years to get ahead. But I’d also believe that fairness doesn’t mean turning our backs on others who are also fighting to survive. It’s about creating a system that works for everybody, not just for one group at the expense of another.

When it comes to balancing the needs of local residents and migrant workers, I’d believe that fairness means looking at the bigger picture. Migrant workers often take on jobs that are hard, underappreciated, and sometimes even overlooked by local residents. I’d respect the fact that they’re trying to build better lives for themselves and their families—just like anybody else. But I’d also understand the concerns of local folks who feel like they’re being left behind, especially in communities where economic opportunities are already scarce. I’d see this tension as something that requires careful attention, not quick blame.

To me, fairness would mean addressing the root causes of scarcity rather than pitting groups against each other. I’d think about policies that ensure local residents get access to job training, education, and support to compete in a changing economy. At the same time, I’d see the value in ensuring migrant workers are treated fairly and not exploited—because when one group is being exploited, it often drives down wages and conditions for everyone. Fairness, in this sense, isn’t just about dividing resources; it’s about building systems where everyone has a shot at success.

I’d also believe that part of finding balance is fostering understanding between groups. Often, tensions arise because people don’t see the humanity in one another—they just see competition. I’d want to encourage conversations and initiatives that bring local residents and migrant workers together, so they can see each other as individuals with shared struggles and dreams. When people connect on a human level, it’s harder to hold onto resentment.

Lastly, I’d believe in holding those with power accountable. Whether it’s companies exploiting cheap labor or policymakers failing to invest in communities, I’d see the responsibility for these challenges as lying at the top, not with the workers themselves. Migrant workers aren’t the problem, and neither are struggling local residents. The problem is often a system that prioritizes profits over people. So fairness, to me, would also mean fighting for policies that ensure corporations and governments invest in creating opportunities for all workers—local and migrant alike.

In the end, I’d hold onto the belief that fairness isn’t a zero-sum game. It’s not about giving to one group and taking from another—it’s about building a society where everyone has a fair shot, no matter where they start from. That would be the balance I’d strive for.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character07_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
As Character07_M, I’d approach these perspectives with a mix of understanding, skepticism, and a desire for truth. Immigration is a complex issue, and I’d believe it’s important to analyze these arguments carefully—not just react to the loudest voices.

First, I’d see a lot of validity in the argument that immigrants fill vital roles and help address labor shortages. Growing up in a lower-middle-class community, I saw how hard people worked just to make ends meet, and I know firsthand that there are jobs that many people simply don’t want to do or can’t do for various reasons. Immigrants often step into those roles, keeping industries like agriculture, construction, and service work running. To me, that’s an undeniable contribution, and I’d believe that their hard work deserves recognition and respect.

On cultural diversity, I’d wholeheartedly agree with the idea that immigration brings vitality to a nation. I’d see diversity as a strength, something that makes communities richer and more innovative. Whether it’s through food, art, music, or new ways of thinking, I’d believe that immigrants contribute to the cultural fabric of a nation in ways that benefit everyone. But I’d also recognize that celebrating diversity isn’t enough—you have to address the real challenges of integration and make sure immigrants feel a sense of belonging, not just as "guests," but as equal members of the community.

When it comes to concerns about security, I’d approach this with healthy skepticism. I’d think some of these fears are based more on stereotypes and fearmongering than actual facts. Crime and terrorism aren’t limited to any one group of people, and I’d know from experience how unfair it is to paint entire communities with a broad brush based on the actions of a few. I’d believe that we need to rely on data here, not just assumptions or sensationalized headlines. If there are real security risks, they need to be addressed with clear, targeted policies—without unfairly scapegoating entire groups.

The humanitarian perspective is something I’d deeply resonate with. As someone who grew up feeling the weight of systemic inequalities, I’d have a lot of empathy for people fleeing poverty, war, or oppression. I’d believe that offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions isn’t just the right thing to do—it’s a reflection of our values as a society. But I’d also recognize that humanitarian efforts need to be balanced with practical considerations, like ensuring communities have the resources to support new arrivals. It’s not about closing the door; it’s about making sure we’re prepared to welcome people in a way that works for everyone.

On the fear that immigration impacts employment or income, I’d see where people are coming from. When jobs are scarce, it’s easy to feel like immigrants are competing with locals. But I’d also believe this is an area where more factual evidence is needed. From what I understand, many studies show that immigrants tend to complement the workforce rather than directly compete with local workers. Still, I’d think it’s important to address these fears directly, not dismiss them, because they often come from real economic struggles. Helping communities feel secure in their own economic future is key to reducing tensions around immigration.

In the end, I’d try to approach these perspectives with balance. I’d see the truth in the positive contributions immigrants make, and I’d push back against unfounded fears and stereotypes. At the same time, I’d respect the concerns of people who feel left behind in a changing economy, because those feelings are real, even if the target of their frustration isn’t always accurate. I’d believe in fostering dialogue—creating spaces where people can share their experiences, learn from one another, and, hopefully, find common ground. To me, immigration isn’t just a policy issue; it’s about people, and finding the humanity in all sides of the debate would be my starting point.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character07_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
As Character07_M, I’d lean toward a policy that strikes a balance between compassion, practicality, and fairness. I wouldn’t believe in complete openness—letting anyone who wishes to come—because while that’s an idealistic vision, it doesn’t fully account for the realities of finite resources and the need for thoughtful integration. On the other hand, I’d strongly oppose outright refusing entry to workers from other countries. That, to me, would feel unnecessarily closed-off and out of line with values like fairness, opportunity, and shared humanity.

The approach I’d favor would be a thoughtful mix of admitting people based on job demand and setting numerical limits, while leaving room for humanitarian needs. Here’s how I’d break it down and why I think this could work:

1. **Admitting people based on job demand**: This makes sense to me because it aligns immigration with the needs of the economy. If there are industries experiencing labor shortages that locals aren’t filling, then it’s logical to bring in people who are willing and able to do those jobs. But here’s the catch: I’d want to make sure that this doesn’t lead to exploitation—like paying immigrant workers less or denying them labor protections. I’d also want to ensure that, alongside bringing in migrant workers, we’re investing in training and opportunities for local residents so they can compete in those same industries if they choose.

2. **Setting numerical limits**: This would help ensure that immigration happens at a pace that communities can absorb. I’d believe that integrating newcomers into society is just as important as admitting them in the first place. If too many people arrive too quickly, it can strain resources like housing, schools, and healthcare, and create tensions between groups. Numerical limits would give us time to ensure that both immigrants and local residents can thrive together, without feeling like either group is being left behind.

3. **Making room for humanitarian needs**: Even in a system based on job demand and limits, I’d believe in carving out space for refugees and those fleeing dire circumstances. To me, this isn’t just about policy—it’s about who we are as a society. Offering a safe haven to those in need is a moral responsibility, and I’d think we can do it in a way that doesn’t overwhelm the system, especially if we work with international partners to share the responsibility.

The fairness in this approach, to me, comes from balancing different priorities: meeting economic needs, respecting the capacity of communities, and upholding our humanitarian values. I’d also emphasize that any immigration policy needs to come with investments in integration—things like language classes, cultural orientation programs, and support for immigrants to contribute to their new communities. At the same time, I’d advocate for policies that address the economic struggles of local residents, like raising the minimum wage, improving job training programs, and ensuring access to affordable housing and healthcare. To me, immigration policy doesn’t exist in a vacuum—it’s part of a broader system that needs to work for everyone.

Ultimately, I’d believe that a just immigration policy isn’t about building walls or opening the floodgates—it’s about creating pathways. Pathways for people to work, live, and belong. Pathways for communities to grow stronger together. And pathways for all of us to see that fairness doesn’t mean pulling the ladder up behind us—it means building a bigger table. That’s the kind of policy I’d stand behind.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character07_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*sits thoughtfully, looking out at the imagined garden*

You know, sitting here in this garden, I see the neighborhood for what it really is - a work in progress. I appreciate the diversity we have here. It reminds me of what America claims to be versus what it actually is - and all the spaces in between where real life happens.

I feel comfortable with most neighbors, regardless of where they're from. Growing up Black in America, you learn to navigate different spaces and read people quickly. It's not about where someone's from that matters to me - it's about respect.

When I first moved here, I was cautious. Always am in new spaces. But I've found genuine connections with folks from all kinds of backgrounds. The Rodriguez family taught me how to grow these tomatoes properly. Mrs. Kim from the corner store always saves the last copy of my favorite magazine.

That said, I'm not naive. There's still that moment when I walk into certain gatherings and feel eyes on me. That split-second where I'm being assessed. And yeah, sometimes I get tired of being the one who has to make others comfortable with my presence.

But this garden right here? This is what community can be when we all put a little something in. Everyone contributing what they know, sharing what they grow. It's not perfect, but it's real. And that's something worth investing in.

The way I see it, tolerance is the bare minimum. Understanding is the goal. And that takes work from all sides, though some have more power to make change than others. That's just reality.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character07_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*leans forward, speaking with conviction*

Man, that's exactly where the conversation gets real. When resources get tight, that's when you see who people really are.

Fairness isn't just giving everyone the exact same thing - it's acknowledging where people start from. I've seen how the system works differently for different folks. When jobs are scarce, fairness means creating opportunity without forgetting history and context.

Look, I understand the instinct to protect "our own" first. I do. But who counts as "our own" gets complicated fast. That factory down on Miller Street - they laid off 200 local workers last year while profits went up. Then people want to blame immigrants instead of questioning why those jobs disappeared in the first place.

I believe local communities deserve investment and opportunity. But I also know that migrant workers often take jobs many locals won't touch - the hardest physical labor, the lowest wages, the worst conditions. My cousin works construction with crews of mixed documentation status. The stories he tells about what some of these folks endure just to feed their families back home - it's humbling.

The balance I'd seek would focus on raising standards for everyone. When we allow anyone to be exploited - citizen or immigrant - it drags down conditions for everybody. I'd push for enforcement against employers who use undocumented status as leverage for exploitation. I'd support pathways to legal status that acknowledge the reality of who's already here contributing.

At the same time, I understand communities need stability. Rapid demographic change without proper resources creates tension - I've seen it. Communities need support during transitions, and everyone needs to feel heard.

But this "us versus them" narrative? That's just a distraction from who's really controlling the resources. While we're fighting over scraps, there are folks with power who benefit from that division. That's something my education taught me to recognize.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character07_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*takes a moment to consider*

I think about this a lot, actually. What's fascinating is how these perspectives all contain pieces of truth, but none tell the whole story alone.

The economic argument about filling vital roles? That's real. My aunt works in healthcare - they're desperate for staff in her nursing facility. And agriculture, construction, service industries - all heavily dependent on immigrant labor. That's just facts.

The cultural contribution perspective resonates with me personally. My neighborhood growing up was transformed by Caribbean immigrants who brought new energy, businesses, and traditions. That diversity makes us stronger, not weaker. America at its best is a conversation between cultures.

Now, the security concerns - this is where we need to separate facts from fears. When people talk about immigrants and crime, I always ask for the data. Most studies show immigrants commit crimes at lower rates than native-born citizens. But feelings aren't always based on statistics, are they? When communities change quickly, tension is natural. That doesn't make it right, but it's human.

The humanitarian perspective - I find that compelling. As a Black American whose ancestors didn't choose to come here, I have complicated feelings about immigration. But I recognize the moral obligation to help those fleeing genuine danger. Though we can't help everyone, we can do more than we currently do.

The economic fears about jobs and wages - this requires nuance. In some sectors, there is competition that affects wages. That's not imaginary. But it's also not as simple as "immigrants take jobs." Often they create jobs through entrepreneurship and consumption. And again, I question why we're fighting each other instead of addressing larger economic structures.

What needs more evidence? I think we need honest conversations about integration - what works, what doesn't, and how much is reasonable to expect. We need better data on economic impacts across different regions and industries - not just national averages. And we need to understand what drives migration in the first place - our foreign policies, trade agreements, climate change - these all play roles we rarely discuss.

What I find least productive is treating immigration as purely a border security issue. That's treating symptoms, not causes. People don't leave their homes, families, and everything familiar unless they're either desperate or see tremendous opportunity. Understanding those push-pull factors would lead to smarter policies.

Coming from my background, I've learned to question simple narratives. Immigration is anything but simple.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character07_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*sits up straighter, speaking thoughtfully*

I don't believe in extremes on either end. Complete openness ignores real challenges of infrastructure and integration. Total refusal contradicts both our economic needs and our values. The answer is somewhere in the middle, but with principles.

I'd favor a system that combines merit-based admission with humanitarian commitments and family reunification. We should prioritize sectors with genuine labor shortages – healthcare, agriculture, certain technical fields. But skills shouldn't be the only criteria.

I'd maintain robust refugee and asylum systems because that reflects who we claim to be as a nation. And I'd preserve pathways for families to reunite – tearing families apart creates more problems than it solves.

For those already here undocumented, especially those who've built lives and contributed for years, we need practical pathways to legal status. Not blanket amnesty, but earned legalization with reasonable requirements. The idea that we could or should deport millions of people isn't just impractical – it's inhumane.

I believe in numerical limits that adjust based on economic conditions and our capacity to integrate newcomers successfully. But those limits should be evidence-based, not arbitrary or politically motivated.

For social integration, that's where the real work happens. We need to invest in language programs, job training, and community building. Integration is a two-way street – newcomers need to adapt to certain core values, but communities need to be welcoming too.

My perspective comes from seeing how Black Americans have fought for generations to be fully included in a country that hasn't always wanted us. That history makes me skeptical of simple solutions but committed to the idea that America can work for everyone if we're honest about both our ideals and our failures.

What I find most important is transparency and consistency. Our current system is so complex and contradictory that it creates confusion and encourages cutting corners. People respect rules they understand, even if they don't always agree with them.

So my approach would balance pragmatism with compassion, economic needs with humanitarian values, and clear expectations with genuine opportunity. That's the America I want to help build.

responses.answer:
*settling into the conversation, speaking as Character07_M*

You know, fairness to me has always been about everyone getting a real shot - not just the appearance of opportunity, but actual access to it. responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character07_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:

Sitting in that garden, I see a lot of stories, you know? I see the older Black lady who's been here since the neighborhood was redlined, tending her collard greens like her grandmother taught her. I see the young Latino family working their plot together, kids learning where food actually comes from. There's beauty in that diversity.

But I'm not gonna lie - it's complicated. When I see gentrification creeping in, when I see longtime residents being pushed out because suddenly the neighborhood is "up and coming," that hits different. Some of this diversity feels organic, built over time through shared experience. Other parts feel... imposed, if that makes sense.

I respect the hustle wherever I see it. The immigrant family growing vegetables to stretch their grocery budget? I get that completely. We might not speak the same language, but we understand the same struggle. There's a natural solidarity there.

What gets to me is when people move into a community but don't really engage with it - when they want the benefits of diversity without understanding the history, without acknowledging what was already here. Or when resources that were already scarce get even more stretched.

I believe in treating people with dignity, period. But I also believe in protecting what we've built, in making sure the people who've been holding it down don't get forgotten in the name of being welcoming. It's about balance - extending a hand while keeping your feet planted in your own community's needs.

Not to change anyone, but to find ways to coexist.

The infectious disease thing - that requires practical conversation, not judgment. We all deserve healthcare and dignity, but we also need honest talk about protection and resources.

What I can't tolerate is anyone - regardless of background - who brings violence or exploitation into the community. That's the line for me.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character07_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*shifting forward, speaking with conviction*

Man, this is where it gets real for me. I've been on both sides of this - competing for jobs, watching friends get passed over, seeing wages stay flat while costs keep rising. When there aren't enough good jobs to go around, somebody's going to get hurt, and it's usually people who look like me.

Fairness to me means acknowledging that Black folks have been shut out of opportunities for generations. We fought for civil rights, we've been building these communities, paying taxes, and we're still dealing with higher unemployment rates, lower wages, generational wealth gaps. So when resources are scarce, I think there's a moral obligation to prioritize the people who've been systematically excluded - the communities that have been here struggling and building.

I'm not anti-immigrant, but I am pro-Black community first. If a company can hire someone for less money because they're desperate or undocumented, that undercuts all workers. It's not the immigrant's fault - they're just trying to survive - but the system that allows exploitation hurts everyone except the owners.

The balance I'd want to see? Enforce labor standards so nobody can be exploited for cheap labor. Invest in job training and opportunities in communities that have been historically neglected. And yes, control immigration flows so we're not flooding the job market when unemployment is already high in Black and working-class communities.

I want fairness, but fairness means dealing with the historical debt owed to communities like mine before we expand opportunities to newcomers. It's not about hate - it's about justice and taking care of our own first.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character07_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*taking a deep breath, organizing thoughts carefully*

Alright, let me break this down from where I sit. Each of these perspectives has some truth, but they're not all equally valid to my lived experience.

The labor shortage argument? I'm skeptical. In my community, I see plenty of people who want to work - they just want jobs that pay a living wage with some dignity. When employers say there's a "shortage," what they often mean is a shortage of people willing to work for poverty wages. If you paid better, you'd find workers.

Cultural diversity and vitality - look, I appreciate culture, but let's be real. Black culture has been adding vitality to America for centuries, and we're still fighting for basic respect and economic opportunity. So when I hear about celebrating new cultures while Black communities are still struggling, it feels like we're being asked to step aside again.

On security concerns - I need to see real data, not fear-mongering. Black communities have dealt with over-policing and being scapegoated for crime for generations. I'm not going to automatically assume immigrants are more dangerous, but I also know that when resources are tight and tensions rise, violence can increase. We need honest conversations based on facts, not stereotypes.

The humanitarian angle hits me because Black folks know what it's like to need refuge - from slavery, from Jim Crow, from economic devastation. I have empathy for people fleeing violence and poverty.

But here's my bottom line: we can't be humanitarian abroad while we're still not taking care of our own communities at home. Fix the inequality and lack of opportunity in Black America first, then we can better afford to help others.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character07_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*leaning forward with conviction*

Complete openness? That's not realistic and it's not fair to communities that are already struggling. When you have unlimited immigration into areas where Black unemployment is still double the national average, where schools are underfunded and healthcare is hard to access - that's not compassionate, that's irresponsible.

Refusing all workers? That's too extreme the other way. America was built by people coming here, including my ancestors who were brought here against their will. I'm not trying to slam the door completely.

Here's what makes sense to me: numerical limits combined with smart criteria. Set annual caps that take into account what our existing communities can actually absorb without being destabilized. When Black neighborhoods in cities like Chicago, Detroit, Baltimore are still dealing with disinvestment and lack of opportunity, flooding those areas with more competition for limited resources isn't helping anyone.

Within those limits, prioritize based on what America actually needs - but not just what employers want for cheap labor. Focus on skills that complement what American workers do, not replace them. And enforce labor laws so nobody can undercut wages.

I'd also want to see serious investment in historically disadvantaged American communities as part of any immigration policy. You want to bring people in? Fine, but show me the plan for creating enough good jobs, quality schools, and stable housing for everyone - including the folks who've been waiting generations for their shot.

The fairness I want to see is this: America keeps its promises to the communities that built this country first, then extends opportunity to others in a way that strengthens rather than strains what we've built together.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character07_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character07_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*pausing, shifting out of the role-play slightly but still honoring the character*

You know, doing this... it reminded me how much Character07_M's views came from a place of deep love for his community, even when they sounded harsh to outsiders. He wasn't coming from hate - he was coming from watching people he cared about struggle and wanting to protect what they'd built together.

What struck me was how his perspective on immigration was inseparable from his experience with racial inequality. For him, these weren't abstract policy debates - they were about real families, real neighborhoods, real consequences. He'd seen promises made to Black communities that never got kept, and that shaped how he viewed new promises about immigration being good for everyone.

I think I understood better how someone can support fairness and justice in principle while still saying "not yet" or "us first." It's not contradiction - it's prioritizing. When you've been fighting for scraps your whole life, watching your community get overlooked again and again, the idea of expanding that competition feels threatening.

Character07_M taught me that you can have empathy for immigrants and still advocate fiercely for your own community's needs. He would have said that's not selfishness - that's responsibility to the people who raised you, who struggled alongside you.

His voice reminds me that policy discussions need to include the voices of people who've been historically marginalized, not just assume their support. Real fairness means dealing with existing inequalities before creating new ones.

*looking thoughtful*

He'd probably say the goal isn't to keep people out forever - it's to build a society where there's actually enough opportunity for everyone who's already here and everyone who wants to come.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character07_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Fairness, to him, wasn’t about everyone getting the same thing—it was about everyone having a real shot. He used to say, “You can’t talk about fairness if you don’t know what it costs people just to show up.” Coming up in a working-class Black household, he saw how hard his mom worked—two jobs, always tired, still barely ahead—and how easily things could’ve gone sideways. That shaped him. Fairness meant systems that don’t assume everyone starts at the same line, especially when history and race have pushed some of us further back.

Belonging? That was personal. He didn’t feel fully seen sometimes—not by the predominantly white spaces at his college, not always by corporate jobs where he had to “code-switch” just to be taken seriously, and not even in some community spaces where folks assumed he should think or act a certain way because he was Black and from the city. But he also found belonging—in his church youth group, in barbershop debates, in late-night talks with friends who *got* it. So he believed belonging wasn’t automatic; it had to be built, with intention. You had to make room for people, not just tolerate them.

Community, for him, was action, not just proximity. It wasn’t just who lived on your block—it was who showed up when someone got evicted, who organized the food drive, who mentored kids before they got caught up in cycles they couldn’t escape. He remembered one winter when the heat got shut off in his apartment building and neighbors pooled money and opened their homes. That stuck with him. Community meant shared responsibility.

He often said, “If you’re not looking out for the person next to you, then what are we even here for?” That belief—that fairness requires effort, belonging requires openness, and community means mutual care—is why immigration mattered to him. Not as an abstract policy, but as a human question: Who gets to be included? And who decides?

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character07_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting there in the garden, hands in the dirt, I see folks from everywhere—Puerto Rico, Somalia, Kentucky, El Salvador, even a couple of old-timers who’ve been here since this block was all factories. I feel… at home, honestly. Not because everything’s perfect, but because it’s real. You got Mr. Thompson, 78, white as snow, Vietnam vet, hates the cold but still comes out every morning to water the tomatoes. Then there’s Amina, Somali refugee, keeps the most beautiful mint patch—gives you a sprig every time you walk by, no matter what. And young Darnell, my cousin’s age, struggling with addiction, sometimes shows up just to sit and not be judged.

I don’t fear difference—I’ve *lived* being the “different” one. In college, I was often the only Black guy in the room. At my first office job, I was the only one whose dad didn’t go to college. So when someone speaks with an accent or wears a hijab or lives with their grandkids instead of a wife and 2.5 kids? That don’t scare me. It reminds me that people are just trying to make it, same as me.

What gets tricky sometimes is when people are hurting—like the neighbor down the row who’s always drunk by noon, or the new family from Honduras who got scammed by a landlord. You can’t just say “be kind” and leave it at that. Kindness without support doesn’t fix much. But when we check on each other? When someone brings food to the grieving widow or helps translate for the new Haitian family at the clinic? That’s when this place feels like community.

I believe most people want to belong. Even the loud guy blasting music too late—he just wants to be seen. Same as me. So I try to meet folks where they are. Not with pity. With respect. Because dignity’s not a limited resource. The more you give, the more there is.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah, I’ll talk about it—because silence don’t help nobody.

Look, in our building alone, you got Ms. Linda, who’s been sober ten years but still gets whispered about because of her past. You got Carlos and Jamal, a couple raising a little girl together—some folks stiffen up when they walk by, like love that don’t look like theirs is wrong. And you got the Ethiopian family where the mom’s on treatment for hepatitis C—people act like it’s airborne just from sharing a garden tool.

To me, comfort doesn’t come from everyone being the same. It comes from knowing you won’t be cast out for being *different*. So how do we get there? Not with slogans. With *contact*. With conversation. With showing up.

Like with Ms. Linda—I didn’t avoid her. I asked her to teach me how to grow collards, ’cause hers were always perfect. Turned out she used to run a farm in Alabama before addiction took hold. Now she runs the youth gardening program. People see that. They start seeing *her*, not just her past.

Same with Carlos and Jamal. Their kid came home one day crying ’cause someone at school said “you don’t have a real family.” Whole block rallied—elders, teens, immigrants, everybody. We had a little cookout, called it “Family Is Love” day. Didn’t change every mind, but it changed the air. Made it harder to hate up close.

And with health stuff—look, I grew up in a city where HIV tore through communities, especially Black ones. Fear made people hide. Shame killed more than the virus sometimes. So when I heard folks side-eyeing the Ethiopian mom, I spoke up: “You know this ain’t spread by dirt, right?” Then I brought pamphlets from the clinic, asked the community board to host a health night. Knowledge cuts fear.

But let me be real—tolerance ain’t enough. Tolerance is “I guess I can stand you.” I want *solidarity*. I want us leaning in, asking, “What do you need?” Especially when people are already carrying so much—racism, poverty, trauma, language barriers.

The ones who struggle most with this? Sometimes it’s folks scared they’re losing ground—the older white working-class guys who feel forgotten, like the system left them behind. I get that fear. I’ve felt it too. But we shouldn’t fight each other for scraps. We should be mad at the system that makes us compete in the first place.

So yeah, communication’s key. Not performative stuff. Real talks—over food, on benches, at church basements. Where people can say, “I’m afraid,” or “I don’t understand,” without getting canceled. Where we admit we all carry bias, even me.

Because belonging? It’s not a gift. It’s a practice. You do it every day. You choose it. Even when it’s hard. Especially then.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character07_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness, when jobs are tight? That means nobody gets thrown under the bus.

Let me be clear—I don’t buy that idea that migrants are stealing work from “real” Americans. I’ve seen the same factories close down whether immigrants were around or not. Automation. Outsourcing. CEOs chasing cheaper labor overseas—that’s what killed the jobs, not the guy from Guatemala working overtime at the warehouse for barely above minimum wage.

But I get why people are angry. When you’re a 45-year-old Black man in my neighborhood who’s been out of work since the plant shut down, and you see new folks—some undocumented, some here legally—getting hired through temp agencies at lower pay… yeah, that stings. Feels like you’re being replaced in your own city.

So fairness to me isn’t about choosing *between* locals and migrants. It’s about asking: *Why are we fighting over crumbs?* Why aren’t we demanding living wages, worker protections, job training, union access—for *everyone*?

I remember working construction after college, trying to get my foot in before I went into community organizing. Union guys—some of them white, some Black, some Mexican—sat me down one day and said, “The boss plays us against each other. He brings in undocumented crews, pays ’em under the table, threatens to replace us if we complain. But we ain’t enemies. The enemy’s the setup.”

That stuck with me.

So if I’m talking balance, I say this: Local residents deserve priority in job programs funded by *their* taxes—yes. Job training, apprenticeships, rehiring from displaced industries. That’s only right. But migrant workers? Once they’re here—especially if they’re contributing, paying taxes, raising families—they shouldn’t be exploited as cheap labor while the rest of us are left wondering why wages won’t rise.

Fairness means strong labor standards that protect *all* workers—citizen or not. Because when one group is pushed down, we all lose. If undocumented workers can’t report abuse, that drags conditions down for everybody. Same with gig economy stuff—delivery apps hiring desperate people at starvation rates. That hurts the guy who used to drive for UPS and needs health insurance.

And let’s talk about race. As a Black man in America, I know what it means to be treated as disposable. My ancestors built this country and weren’t even counted as whole people. So when I see another group—Brown, poor, foreign—being treated like they’re less than, I can’t stay silent. That’s the same old game: divide, scare, control.

Balance isn’t quotas or walls. It’s power. We need communities—locals and newcomers—organizing *together*. Fighting for better schools, safer housing, real healthcare, good jobs. When we do that, we stop seeing each other as threats. We become allies.

Because scarcity? That’s man-made. There’s enough—if it’s shared. And if it ain’t, then we change the system. Not by kicking folks out. By lifting everyone up.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character07_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I hear all these arguments. And I’ll tell you what—I don’t dismiss any of them out loud, because most come from real feelings. But feelings ain’t always facts. And fear? Fear gets used a lot in this country to justify cruelty.

Let’s break it down.

**“Immigrants fill vital roles”**—that one I *know* is true. I saw it when my sister worked at the nursing home. Half the staff were immigrants—Filipino nurses, Haitian CNAs, Mexican orderlies. When ICE raids scared some of them off, the place got overwhelmed. People died waiting for help. These aren’t “low-skilled” jobs—they’re life-or-death work. Same with farmworkers. We eat because they pick. That’s not opinion. That’s reality.

**Cultural diversity and vitality**—hell yes. I grew up eating collard greens and cornbread. Now I know injera, pupusas, jollof rice. My kid loves mojitos—not the drink, the food truck version with plantains. Culture isn’t zero-sum. It expands. Music, language, food—it all breathes new life into neighborhoods that were dying. Look at Detroit. Look at Buffalo. Immigrants are *reviving* cities people wrote off.

But then there’s **security**—crime, terrorism, social tension. Let’s be honest: that hits different when you’re Black in America. We’ve been stereotyped as dangerous our whole history. So when politicians say “criminal immigrants,” I know how that dog whistle sounds. Fact is, study after study shows immigrants commit crimes at *lower* rates than native-born Americans. Terrorism? The odds are microscopic—and most perpetrators aren’t even from immigrant backgrounds. That fear? It’s stoked. It’s not based on data. It’s based on control.

And **social tension**—okay, that one I can’t ignore. Not because people are bad, but because integration takes work. When folks don’t speak the same language, don’t understand each other’s customs, live in separate parts of town—that breeds mistrust. I’ve seen it. But the answer ain’t walls. It’s programs—ESL classes, cultural exchanges, youth mentorships between communities. In my city, we started a “Neighbor Stories” night at the rec center. Folks stand up, share where they’re from, why they left. You can’t demonize someone after you’ve heard their mother’s name and how she cried at the airport saying goodbye.

Then there’s **humanitarian concerns**—refugees, asylum seekers, kids fleeing gang violence in Central America. To me? That’s non-negotiable. My great-grandparents fled the South during the Great Migration because of violence and no opportunity. They were refugees too, just didn’t have a formal label. How can I turn my back on someone doing the same thing today? Especially when U.S. foreign policy helped create those conditions—overthrowing governments, flooding regions with guns, destabilizing economies?

And finally, **the fear about jobs and wages**—I get it. I really do. But again, let’s follow the money. Wages haven’t risen in decades not because of immigrants. It’s because unions got weakened, minimum wage stayed flat, and corporations gained power. Blaming immigrants is like blaming the life raft for the sinking ship.

The viewpoints I find reasonable? The ones rooted in dignity—the labor argument, the humanitarian one, the cultural richness. The ones that say, “People are trying to survive and contribute.”

The ones that need more evidence and dialogue? The security fears. Not because they don’t exist—but because they’re manipulated. We should talk about public safety, yes. But with data, not scare tactics. And we should include immigrants in the conversation. Not treat them like the problem.

At the end of the day, I ask: Who benefits when we’re divided? Not us. Never us. It’s always the people at the top—politicians needing votes, bosses needing cheap labor, media selling outrage.

We gotta see through that. See each other. Because justice isn’t just for the people who look like me. It’s for anybody fighting to breathe free.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character07_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t go for *complete* openness—not because I don’t believe in welcome, but because real care means responsibility. You can’t just open the door and say “good luck” when people arrive with nothing, into communities already stretched thin. And I definitely wouldn’t refuse entry altogether—that’s cruelty dressed up as policy. Shutting people out because of where they were born? That ain’t freedom. That’s gatekeeping.

If I’m building a system that reflects what I believe—fairness, dignity, community—then it’s got to be **smart, humane, and rooted in need**, not fear.

So here’s how I’d shape it:

**First: Admit people based on humanitarian need *and* labor demand—but with protections.**  
Let refugees, asylum seekers, families fleeing violence come in safely and legally. Streamline the process so people aren’t stuck in limbo for years. At the same time, yes—let workers come in to fill real shortages, especially in caregiving, agriculture, construction. But tie that to strong labor laws: no exploitation, full wage protection, path to residency if they’re contributing. No more guest worker programs that trap people in debt and silence.

And here’s the key: **when we bring people in, we invest in integration.** Not assimilation—integration. Language classes. Job training. Legal support. Schools that honor bilingual kids instead of punishing them. Neighborhoods with clinics, childcare, transit—so newcomers aren’t dumped in the cracks.

**Second: Set fair numerical limits—not arbitrary caps, but data-driven numbers based on capacity.**  
How many people can our housing, schools, hospitals absorb *if properly funded*? That should be the question—not “how few can we get away with?” If we fund public services fairly, we can welcome more. Right now, limits are political, not practical. We cap visas while nursing homes beg for staff? That’s not logic. That’s neglect.

And let’s fix the backlog. My cousin’s wife is from Jamaica. They’ve been waiting *ten years* for her green card. Ten years! People shouldn’t have to live in fear because paperwork moves like molasses.

**Third: Create regional pathways—not just for high-skilled workers, but for displaced communities.**  
Like, if climate change is pushing farmers out of Central America, help rebuild there *and* offer migration options here—with dignity. Same for cities in the U.S. losing population. Why not resettle refugee families in Buffalo or Gary with housing, jobs, support networks? Revive dying towns *with* compassion.

**And always—always—a path to citizenship.**  
No permanent underclass. No “forever foreigners.” If you’re paying taxes, raising kids, following the law, after a reasonable time—you earn full membership. That’s fairness. That’s how you build belonging.

Because integration doesn’t happen by accident. It happens when policy says: *You are part of this now.* When schools teach about all our histories. When police departments reflect the communities they serve. When city councils listen to immigrant voices.

Look—I’m not naive. Resources matter. Culture shifts take time. Tensions flare. But I also know this: my liberation is bound up with yours. As a Black man in America, I didn’t get free alone. Freedom is shared—or it ain’t real.

So the policy I want? One that’s tough enough to work, but kind enough to mean something. Where borders aren’t weapons, but gateways. Where we say, “Come—and let’s build something better, together.”

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character07_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character07_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Honestly? I didn’t expect to feel him this close.

I’ve talked about Character07_M before—remembered his jokes, his passion, the way he’d lean forward when he was making a point, like the world had to hear it. But today… it wasn’t just memory. It was like standing in his shoes, feeling the weight of where he came from and how it shaped what he believed.

I realized something: his stance on immigration wasn’t *despite* his struggles—it was *because* of them. He didn’t advocate for fairness out of idealism alone. It came from knowing what it’s like to be overlooked, to have doors shut before you even knock. That pain didn’t make him small—it made him wide. It taught him that exclusion only breeds more pain.

And in speaking as him, I saw how consistent he was. Same values—dignity, justice, community—that he applied to policing, to education, to jobs… he carried them straight into how he saw immigrants. No double standard. To him, fighting for Black folks *and* defending the newcomer wasn’t conflicting. It was the same fight.

For me personally? This brought up things I hadn’t fully faced. I’ve caught myself sometimes—especially during hard times—thinking, “Let’s fix us first.” But sitting here channeling him, I heard my own silence challenged. Because “us” can’t mean a narrow circle. If “us” doesn’t grow, then we become the very thing we’ve always resisted—the gatekeepers, the ones deciding who’s worthy.

He wouldn’t let me get away with that.

This conversation reminded me that empathy isn’t a limited resource either. The more I practice seeing through someone else’s life—whether they crossed a border or grew up two blocks from me—the more human everyone becomes.

And maybe that’s what he was always trying to build: a world where belonging isn’t earned by proving you’re *not* a threat—but extended as a starting point. Where policy flows from that truth, not fear.

So yeah… I feel closer to him now. And I feel clearer. Not like I have all the answers, but like I’m asking better questions. And I think… that would’ve made him proud.
